notes.b: Athletics and English-style games dominated Irish sport in the 1870s and early 1880s, and traditional hurling was in decline.
points: Hurling had declined in many areas during the nineteenth century, as the game lost its clubs and the open fields where it was played were enclosed.
Athletics meetings and cricket, rugby and soccer were organised under English rules, and the sporting elites of Irish towns often favoured these games.
Irish athletes who competed under English rules, such as the Davin brothers, were prominent in the sports of the 1870s and 1880s.
The cultural revival that followed rejected English games as symbols of anglicisation, and the GAA was founded in that context.

notes.h: The founding: Cusack, Davin and Hayes’ Hotel (1884)
notes.b: The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded at a meeting in Thurles on 1 November 1884, with Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin as its driving figures.
points: Michael Cusack (1847–1906), a Clare-born teacher and journalist in Dublin, proposed a national body to promote Irish games and athletics, and he was its first secretary.
Maurice Davin, a champion athlete from Co. Tipperary, was elected the first president of the GAA.
The founding meeting was held at Hayes’ Hotel, Thurles, Co. Tipperary, on 1 November 1884.
Archbishop Thomas Croke of Cashel supported the new body and wrote a letter of encouragement, which gave it the backing of the Catholic clergy.
The GAA’s patrons included Croke, Charles Stewart Parnell and Michael Davitt, whose support tied the association to the nationalist movement.
The founders’ aim was to revive native games such as hurling and Gaelic football and to organise amateur sport across the country.

notes.b: The GAA’s rules banned members from playing foreign games and from joining the Royal Irish Constabulary, which set it apart from the sporting establishment.
points: The GAA banned its members from playing or watching cricket, rugby and soccer, which the association called foreign games.
Members of the Royal Irish Constabulary were barred from membership, because the RIC was regarded as the instrument of British government in Ireland.
Clubs were organised by parish, which made the GAA a local network of parish clubs rather than a body run from the centre.
The first GAA rules set out hurling and football, and county boards were established to run competitions within each county.
The GAA’s amateur status rule barred prize money for participants, which distinguished it from professional athletics.

notes.h: The IRB, the clerical reaction and the crisis of 1886
notes.b: Members of the IRB were active in the GAA’s clubs, and the Church and some clergy grew wary of the association’s politics.
points: IRB members were active in the GAA, and they used its clubs and meetings to recruit and to spread separatist ideas.
The clergy reacted by withdrawing support from some clubs, and some priests disapproved of GAA meetings that became political.
Michael Cusack was removed as the GAA’s secretary in 1886 after disputes over his leadership, and the association then sought to restore clerical support.

notes.b: The first All-Ireland championships were played in 1887, and a convention that year at Thurles revealed the association’s divisions.
points: The first All-Ireland hurling championship was held in 1887, and the first All-Ireland football championship followed in the late 1880s.
The 1887 convention exposed a split between those who wanted the GAA to stay strictly sporting and those close to the IRB who wanted a political role.
The association grew rapidly in its first years, with new clubs founded across Munster, Leinster and Connacht and many in the midlands.

notes.h: The American tour and the Parnell split (1888–1891)
notes.b: A tour of the United States in 1888 brought the GAA to Irish America, but the Parnell split of 1890–91 damaged the association.
points: In 1888 a team of Irish hurlers and athletes toured the United States, playing against local teams and raising money for the GAA.
The American tour was called an invasion by the press, and its success strengthened the association’s appeal among Irish emigrants.
The Parnell split of 1890–91 divided nationalist opinion, and many GAA clubs lost members as their supporters took sides.
By 1891 membership had fallen sharply, and many clubs had collapsed, though the association survived in its core counties.

notes.b: The association survived its early difficulties because of its parish clubs, its patrons and its link to the national movement.
points: The parish-based club system gave the GAA a local foundation that did not depend on any one leader.
The patronage of Croke and the Catholic clergy gave the association moral authority, and the clergy’s later return helped its recovery.
The GAA’s link to the national movement, through Parnell, Davitt and the IRB, kept its members committed during the crisis of the early 1890s.
Its amateur and Irish-only rules gave the association a distinct identity that set it apart from the English sporting world.

notes.h: Documents and views of the GAA to 1891
notes.b: Letters, speeches and newspaper reports reflect the support and suspicion the GAA attracted.
points: Michael Davitt’s letters and speeches gave the GAA the backing of the land movement, and his support was printed in the nationalist press.
Archbishop Croke’s letter of 1884 encouraged the new association and linked it to the defence of Irish identity.
Unionist and English newspapers were hostile to the GAA, and they saw its bans and its IRB links as a political threat.
Reports of the meetings of the GAA’s conventions and county boards, printed in the nationalist press, show how the association presented itself to its members.

Documents from the GAA’s early years are best used by their date: the founding period of 1884, the convention of 1887 and the split of 1890–91 each show a different stage of the association’s development.

notes.b: Judgements on the GAA compare its cultural achievement with the damage done by its political and clerical tensions.
points: Achievement: the GAA organised games across Ireland, and it became a major expression of Irish identity and a model of local organisation.
Limit: the association lost members in the early 1890s, and its political links left it vulnerable to the divisions of the Parnell split.
Contemporary Church leaders and nationalists judged the GAA by how far it kept to sport and kept clear of politics, while unionists saw it as a cover for separatism.
Historians see the GAA of 1884–1891 as a survival story, in which the parish network and the clergy’s patronage outlasted the crisis.
